claims.text: Severe plastic deformation followed by low-temperature annealing can simultaneously increase yield strength and tensile ductility in a brittle FCC MPEA.
Ambient-temperature severe plastic deformation can produce a nanocrystalline or ultrafine-grained CoCrFeMnNi structure.
High-pressure torsion at room temperature induces deformation twinning in CoCrFeMnNi.
A subsequent low-temperature anneal stabilizes a high density of coherent nanoscale twins.
The combined SPD and low-temperature annealing route avoids detrimental phase decomposition.
CrMnFeCoNi is representative of a room-temperature-brittle MPEA.
The representative CrMnFeCoNi alloy has a single-phase FCC structure.
Single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys have relatively low strength.
Low room-temperature ductility and limited strain hardening in the initial alloy are caused by planar dislocation slip.
Coherent nanoscale twin boundaries impede dislocation motion and thereby strengthen the alloy.
Twin boundaries provide sites for dislocation storage and cross-slip, improving ductility and strain hardening.
A dislocation approaching a twin boundary can dissociate, with one partial transmitting through the boundary and another moving along it.
A hierarchical nanotwinned structure changes deformation from planar slip to a more homogeneous mode.
The more homogeneous deformation mode raises strain-hardening rates and delays premature necking.
The proposed treatment will produce yield strength above 1000 MPa while retaining elongation above 50%.
The processed alloy will retain fracture toughness above 200 MPa m1/2.
Standard annealing or solution treatment of nanocrystalline material typically causes grain growth or brittle sigma-phase formation, reducing ductility or providing insufficient strengthening.
The proposed mechanism is applicable to FCC MPEAs with sufficiently low or moderate stacking-fault energy for twinning.
Annealing above the single-phase stability limit causes phase decomposition, including sigma-phase formation, in HPT-processed material.
The annealing window that avoids decomposition while maximizing twin density varies with alloy composition and initial defect density.
